content: Potassium is an essential dietary nutrient that has been studied for its effects on various health outcomes, including blood pressure, lipid profiles, triglycerides, and cholesterol levels. The World Health Organization (WHO) has conducted systematic reviews to evaluate the role of potassium in preventing and managing chronic diseases, particularly in children. These reviews aim to provide evidence-based guidelines for public health interventions. Dr. Nancy J. Aburto, along with her colleagues Ms. Sarah Hanson, Dr. Anna Ziolkowska, and Ms. Hialy Gutierrez, prepared a systematic review under the WHO Nutrition Policy and Scientific Advice Unit. This review was one of three conducted to inform the development of WHO guidelines on potassium intake. The findings were presented to the WHO Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group, which assisted in interpreting the results and generating evidence-based recommendations. Financial support for the review was provided by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare of Japan and the International Kidney Evaluation Association Japan. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are the leading cause of death globally, accounting for approximately 60% of all deaths and 43% of the global disease burden. Cardiovascular disease (CVD), a major NCD, is responsible for 30% of all deaths worldwide. Hypertension is a significant risk factor for CVD, contributing to nearly half of all coronary heart disease cases and over 60% of strokes. Elevated blood pressure in childhood is strongly associated with hypertension and related morbidities in adulthood, as well as cardiovascular pathology during childhood itself. Addressing elevated blood pressure and other NCD risk factors in children is critical for reducing the global burden of these diseases. Three meta-analyses of trials in adults have shown that increased potassium intake lowers blood pressure. However, no systematic reviews have been conducted to assess the effects of increased potassium intake on health outcomes in children. This gap highlights the need for further research to evaluate the impact of potassium on blood pressure, lipid profiles, and catecholamine levels in pediatric populations. The primary objective of the review was to assess the effects of increased potassium intake in children aged 2–15 years on blood pressure and potential adverse effects, such as changes in lipid levels, cholesterol, and triglycerides. Specific objectives included determining whether higher potassium intake has differential effects compared to lower or usual intake, and whether urinary potassium excretion levels of ≥70 mmol/day, ≥90 mmol/day, or ≥120 mmol/day have greater effects on these outcomes. Urinary potassium excretion is a common and valid method for estimating potassium intake. Data from studies indicate that urinary potassium excretion accounts for approximately 77% of dietary intake. Conversion factors were used to estimate potassium intake from urinary excretion values, with 70 mmol/day corresponding to approximately 91 mmol/day of intake, 90 mmol/day to 117 mmol/day, and 120 mmol/day to 156 mmol/day. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, non-randomized trials, and prospective cohort studies. Studies were included if they involved healthy populations or those at risk of hypertension, with a duration of at least three weeks for trials and one year for cohort studies. Exclusion criteria included studies targeting pregnant individuals, acutely ill patients, or those with HIV infection. The primary outcomes of interest were blood pressure (systolic and/or diastolic) and potential adverse effects, such as increased total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides, decreased HDL cholesterol, and elevated catecholamine levels. Studies were included if they reported at least one of these outcomes and involved children aged 2–15 years. The systematic review process involved searching electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library, as well as the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Additional resources, such as reference lists and unpublished studies, were also considered. Two independent reviewers assessed studies for inclusion, and disagreements were resolved through consensus or consultation with a third party. Data extraction was conducted using standardized templates, with information on study population, intervention, and outcomes independently reviewed by two reviewers. Missing information was sought from study authors. The extracted data included general information about the study, trial characteristics, and outcome measures. This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the effects of increased potassium intake on health outcomes in children, contributing to the development of evidence-based public health guidelines.
